::: callout-note
## In this session you will learn to

1.  Chain steps together with the pipe `%>%`
2.  Standardize column names with `clean_names()` and rename columns with `rename()`
3.  Fix column types (dates, numbers) with `mutate()`
4.  Fix values with `if_else()` and `case_when()`
5.  Create new variables (BMI, age groups)
6.  Combine every cleaning step into one pipeline and save the result

**Before you start:** open the workshop folder in Positron (**File → Open Folder...**) and open `student_scripts/Session 2 - Cleaning_STUDENT.R`. Today starts from the raw files, `raw_data/linelist_raw.xlsx` and `raw_data/measles_raw.csv`, and works through the problem lists you wrote at the end of [Session 1](01-setup-and-first-look.qmd). If you fall behind, ready-made copies of today's results (`linelist_clean.rds` and `measles_clean.rds`) are in `processed_data/`.
:::

You will build **two** cleaned datasets side by side: `linelist_clean` in the Follow along code, and `measles_clean` in the TRY ITs.

# Part 2: The pipe `%>%`

In Session 1, doing two things at once meant putting one function inside another:

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 2.1** — Sort by weight and show 3 rows: first with one function inside another, then with the pipe (the next two code blocks).

Pattern: `DATA %>% STEP_1() %>% STEP_2()`
:::

```{r}
head(arrange(linelist_raw, wt_kg), 3)
```

You read that from the **inside out**: arrange the data, *then* take the head. Every extra step adds another layer of brackets. The **pipe** `%>%` writes the same steps **in order, from left to right**:

```{r}
linelist_raw %>% arrange(wt_kg) %>% head(3)
```

The pipe takes the result on its left and passes it in as the **first argument** of the function on its right. Read it as **"and then"**: *take `linelist_raw`, and then arrange it by weight, and then show the first 3 rows.*

-   Keyboard shortcut: **Shift + Cmd + M** (Mac) or **Shift + Ctrl + M** (Windows)
-   With the pipe, you don't write the data inside each function: `count(linelist_raw, hospital)` becomes `linelist_raw %>% count(hospital)`

## Longer pipelines

Put each step on its own line, with the `%>%` at the **end** of the line. `select()` keeps only the **columns** you name:

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 2.2** — A longer pipeline, one step per line: `select()` `Case ID`, `wt_kg`, and `ht_cm`, then `arrange()` by `wt_kg`, then `head(5)`.
:::

```{r}
linelist_raw %>%
  select(`Case ID`, wt_kg, ht_cm) %>%   # keep three columns
  arrange(wt_kg) %>%                    # sort by weight
  head(5)                               # show the first 5 rows
```

That is three steps, readable top to bottom. Written the Session 1 way, it would be `head(arrange(select(linelist_raw, ...), wt_kg), 5)`.

::: callout-note
You may also see `|>`, the pipe built into R itself. For this workshop they do the same thing.
:::

::: callout-warning
## Common mistakes

-   Put `%>%` at the **end** of a line, not at the start of the next one. R stops at a complete line, so a line starting with `%>%` gives an error.
-   Don't end the last line with `%>%`: R then waits for another step (a `+` appears in the Console). Press **Esc** and remove it.
:::

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT 2 (3 min): the pipe

In Session 1 you wrote `` head(arrange(measles_raw, desc(`Temp (C)`)), 10) ``. Rewrite it with the pipe, and add a `select()` step so you only see `` `Patient ID` `` and `` `Temp (C)` ``.

✅ **Check:** two columns, and the top temperature is 104.7

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution

```{r}
measles_raw %>%
  select(`Patient ID`, `Temp (C)`) %>%
  arrange(desc(`Temp (C)`)) %>%
  head(10)
```

Same answer as in Session 1, but now you can read it in order. From here on, almost every piece of code in the workshop uses the pipe.
:::
:::

# Part 3: Column names

## `clean_names()`

One function (from janitor) makes every name lower case, replaces spaces and dots with `_`, and removes symbols. `"Case ID"` becomes `case_id` — after this, you never need backticks again!

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 3.1** — Create `linelist_clean` from `linelist_raw` with `clean_names()`. Compare `names()` before and after.

Pattern: `NEW_DATA <- OLD_DATA %>% clean_names()`
:::

```{r}
names(linelist_raw)

linelist_clean <- linelist_raw %>%
  clean_names()

names(linelist_clean)
```

## `rename()`

`rename(new_name = old_name)` — the **new** name goes on the left.

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 3.2** — Rename `infection_date` → `date_of_infection`, `date_onset` → `onset_date`, and `hosp_date` → `hospital_date`.

Pattern: `DATA <- DATA %>% rename(NEW_NAME = OLD_NAME, NEW_NAME = OLD_NAME)`
:::

```{r}
linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>%
  rename(
    date_of_infection = infection_date,
    onset_date        = date_onset,
    hospital_date     = hosp_date
  )

names(linelist_clean)
```

::: callout-tip
## One step at a time

We build the clean data step by step. Each step takes the current version, changes one thing, and saves it back with `<-`:

`linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>% STEP()`

If your object gets into a bad state, re-run from the first step (`linelist_clean <- linelist_raw %>% clean_names()`). In Part 8 we put all the steps into one pipeline.
:::

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT 3 (2 min): clean the measles column names

Create `measles_clean` from `measles_raw` with `clean_names()`. What did `` `Temp (C)` `` and `` `Vaccinated?` `` turn into?

✅ **Check:** `names(measles_clean)` includes `"temp_c"` and `"vaccinated"`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution

```{r}
measles_clean <- measles_raw %>%
  clean_names()

names(measles_clean)
```

`` `Temp (C)` `` became `temp_c` and `` `Vaccinated?` `` became `vaccinated`: the parentheses and the `?` are removed, and the space becomes `_`.
:::
:::

# Part 4: Fixing types with `mutate()`

`mutate()` creates a new column or overwrites an existing one: `mutate(column = what_to_put_in_it)`. Use the same name to overwrite a column; a new name to add one.

## Dates

`as.Date()` converts text or date-times to dates.

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 4.1** — Turn `date_of_infection`, `onset_date`, `hospital_date`, and `date_of_outcome` into dates with `as.Date()`.

Pattern: `DATA <- DATA %>% mutate(COLUMN = as.Date(COLUMN), COLUMN = as.Date(COLUMN))`
:::

```{r}
linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>%
  mutate(
    date_of_infection = as.Date(date_of_infection),
    onset_date        = as.Date(onset_date),
    hospital_date     = as.Date(hospital_date),
    date_of_outcome   = as.Date(date_of_outcome)
  )

linelist_clean %>% select(date_of_infection:date_of_outcome) %>% glimpse()
```

::: callout-note
## Dates written in other formats

`as.Date()` expects year-month-day (`"2014-05-13"`). For other formats, the **lubridate** package (part of the tidyverse) has functions named after the order: `dmy("13/05/2014")`, `mdy("05/13/2014")`, `ymd("2014-05-13")`.
:::

## Numbers stored as text

`as.numeric()` turns text like `"56"` into the number 56. Text that isn't a number (like `"unknown"`) becomes `NA`, and R warns you: *"NAs introduced by coercion"*. That warning is fine **if** you expected it.

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 4.2** — Turn `age` into a number with `as.numeric()`.
:::

```{r}
linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>%
  mutate(age = as.numeric(age))

class(linelist_clean$age)
```

::: callout-warning
## Common mistakes

-   Forgetting the `<-` at the start: the result prints in the Console but isn't saved.
:::

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT 4 (3 min): fix the measles types

In `measles_clean`:

a)  make `report_date` a date with `as.Date()`
b)  make `age_years` a number with `as.numeric()`. Which values became `NA`?

✅ **Check:** `summary(measles_clean$age_years)` shows a maximum of 999. Suspicious!

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution

```{r}
measles_clean <- measles_clean %>%
  mutate(
    report_date = as.Date(report_date),
    age_years   = as.numeric(age_years)   # "unknown" becomes NA (the warning is expected)
  )

summary(measles_clean$age_years)
```

The 27 `"unknown"` ages became `NA` — that is what the warning is about. A maximum age of 999 is not a real age; we fix it in the next part.
:::
:::

# Part 5: Fixing values with `if_else()`

`if_else(condition, value_if_TRUE, value_if_FALSE)` checks every row and fixes the values that meet one condition.

## Ages in months → years

"If the unit is months, divide by 12; otherwise keep the age."

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 5.1** — Create `age_years` (ages in months divided by 12).
:::

```{r}
linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>%
  mutate(age_years = if_else(age_unit == "months", age / 12, age))

linelist_clean %>%
  filter(age_unit == "months") %>%
  select(age, age_unit, age_years) %>%
  head()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🤔 Think about it: what would have happened in later analyses if we had skipped this step?

A 6-month-old baby would be counted as 6 years old. All 37 ages recorded in months would be too old, which would shift the age groups and the average age.
:::

## Impossible values → missing

Weights of zero or below are impossible. Instead of deleting the whole row (and losing the patient's age, outcome, and dates), we replace only the bad value with `NA`.

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 5.2** — Replace weights of 0 or below with `NA`.
:::

```{r}
linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>%
  mutate(wt_kg = if_else(wt_kg <= 0, NA, wt_kg))

summary(linelist_clean$wt_kg)
```

::: callout-note
## 🔁 The base R way: `ifelse()` (one letter shorter, one big difference)

Base R has `ifelse()`, and you will see it everywhere. It works the same way **until you use it on dates**. Say we want an "estimated onset" that uses the hospital date when the onset date is missing:

::: follow-along
**🔁 Follow along 5.3** — Estimated onset (`hospital_date` when `onset_date` is missing) with `if_else()` and with `ifelse()`. Compare the first 3 values.
:::

```{r}
if_else(is.na(linelist_clean$onset_date), linelist_clean$hospital_date, linelist_clean$onset_date) %>% head(3)
ifelse(is.na(linelist_clean$onset_date), linelist_clean$hospital_date, linelist_clean$onset_date) %>% head(3)
```

`ifelse()` silently turned the dates into **numbers** (days since 1 January 1970). `if_else()` keeps the type, and gives an error instead of a surprise when the two values have different types. That strictness is why we use `if_else()` in this workshop.
:::

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT 5 (4 min): 999 and Fahrenheit

In `measles_clean`:

a)  999 is a code for "unknown": replace `age_years` of 999 with `NA`
b)  temperatures above 45 were entered in Fahrenheit. Convert them: Celsius = (Fahrenheit − 32) × 5 / 9, rounded to 1 decimal with `round(..., 1)`

✅ **Check:** `summary()` shows `age_years` max 52 and `temp_c` max 40.9

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution

```{r}
measles_clean <- measles_clean %>%
  mutate(
    age_years = if_else(age_years == 999, NA, age_years),
    temp_c    = if_else(temp_c > 45, round((temp_c - 32) * 5 / 9, 1), temp_c)
  )

summary(measles_clean$age_years)
summary(measles_clean$temp_c)
```

The four 999s are now `NA` (31 missing ages in total), and the 27 Fahrenheit temperatures are now in °C, so every temperature is between 36 and 40.9.
:::
:::

# Part 6: Recoding categories with `case_when()`

`case_when()` is `if_else()` for **many** conditions. R checks each line in order and uses the first one that is TRUE:

```
case_when(
  condition_1 ~ new_value_1,
  condition_2 ~ new_value_2,
  .default    = value_for_everything_else
)
```

## Gender

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 6.1** — Recode gender `"m"` → `"male"` and `"f"` → `"female"`. Check with `count()`.
:::

```{r}
linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>%
  mutate(gender = case_when(
    gender == "m" ~ "male",
    gender == "f" ~ "female"
  ))

linelist_clean %>% count(gender)
```

Any row that matches no condition becomes `NA` — here, that is the rows that were already missing.

## Hospital names (using the look-up table)

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 6.2** — Look at `hosp_info` and `count(hospital)`, then create `hospital_name` with `case_when()` + `str_detect()`. Check with `count(hospital, hospital_name)` (the next two code blocks).
:::

```{r}
hosp_info
linelist_clean %>% count(hospital)
```

`str_detect(column, "pattern")` is TRUE when the text **contains** the pattern, so one line catches every misspelling. `|` means "or".

```{r}
linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>%
  mutate(hospital_name = case_when(
    str_detect(hospital, "Central")           ~ "Central Hospital",
    str_detect(hospital, "Military|Mitylira") ~ "Military Hospital",
    str_detect(hospital, "Regional")          ~ "Regional Medical center",
    str_detect(hospital, "Mark")              ~ "St. Mark's Maternity Hospital",
    str_detect(hospital, "HMO")               ~ "HMO Health",
    str_detect(hospital, "Premier")           ~ "Premiere Health",
    .default = "Other/Unknown"
  ))

# Check: every old value next to its new value
linelist_clean %>% count(hospital, hospital_name)
```

::: callout-note
## Other useful text functions (stringr)

`str_to_lower()`, `str_to_upper()`, `str_to_title()` change capitalization (`str_to_title("north")` gives `"North"`) · `str_trim()` removes extra spaces · `str_replace(x, "old", "new")` replaces text. You may need these for the TRY ITs!

To check for any of several exact values, use `%in%`: `sex %in% c("Male", "male", "M")`.
:::

::: callout-warning
## Common mistakes

-   Use `~` (tilde), not `=`, between the condition and the new value
-   Put a comma after each line **except** the last
-   Check every recode with `count(old_column, new_column)`
:::

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT 6 (4 min): sex and vaccinated

In `measles_clean`, recode

-   `sex`: Male / male / M → `"male"`, Female / female / F → `"female"`
-   `vaccinated`: Yes / yes / Y → `"Yes"`, No / no / N / NO → `"No"`, Unknown → `"Unknown"`

Pattern: `COLUMN %in% c("VALUE_1", "VALUE_2") ~ "NEW_VALUE"`

✅ **Check:** `count(sex)` shows female 533, male 642, NA 40; `count(vaccinated)` shows only No, Unknown, Yes

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution

```{r}
measles_clean <- measles_clean %>%
  mutate(
    sex = case_when(
      sex %in% c("Male", "male", "M")     ~ "male",
      sex %in% c("Female", "female", "F") ~ "female"
    ),
    vaccinated = case_when(
      vaccinated %in% c("Yes", "yes", "Y")     ~ "Yes",
      vaccinated %in% c("No", "no", "N", "NO") ~ "No",
      vaccinated == "Unknown"                  ~ "Unknown"
    )
  )

measles_clean %>% count(sex)
measles_clean %>% count(vaccinated)
```

Six spellings of sex became two values (the 40 missing stay `NA`), and eight spellings of vaccinated became three: No 741, Unknown 183, Yes 291.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT 7 (5 min): district

Make `district` one of North, South, East, West, Central.

-   Step 1: `district = str_to_title(district)` fixes the capitals
-   Step 2: `case_when()` + `str_detect()` fixes the misspellings ("Nroth", "Cetnral") and the "... District" versions. Keep `NA` as `NA` (no `.default`).

✅ **Check:** `count(district)` shows exactly 5 districts plus NA (34)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution

```{r}
measles_clean <- measles_clean %>%
  mutate(
    district = str_to_title(district),
    district = case_when(
      str_detect(district, "North|Nroth")     ~ "North",
      str_detect(district, "South")           ~ "South",
      str_detect(district, "East")            ~ "East",
      str_detect(district, "West")            ~ "West",
      str_detect(district, "Central|Cetnral") ~ "Central"
    )
  )

measles_clean %>% count(district)
```

`str_to_title()` turns "north" into "North" first, so each `str_detect()` line only has to catch the misspellings and the "... District" versions. Because there is no `.default`, the 34 missing districts stay `NA`.
:::
:::

# Part 7: Creating new variables

## BMI

`mutate()` can calculate a new column from other columns.

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 7.1** — Calculate `bmi`, then set BMIs below 10 or above 60 to `NA` (the next two code blocks).
:::

```{r}
linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>%
  mutate(bmi = round(wt_kg / (ht_cm / 100)^2, 1))

summary(linelist_clean$bmi)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🤔 Think about it: a BMI of 1,250?

That is impossible: the heights and weights don't fit together. Set BMIs outside a plausible range (10–60) to `NA`.
:::

```{r}
linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>%
  mutate(bmi = if_else(bmi < 10 | bmi > 60, NA, bmi))

summary(linelist_clean$bmi)
```

About 1,400 BMIs are now `NA`, because many height and weight values in this teaching dataset are unrealistic. Setting only the bad value to `NA` (instead of filtering out those rows) keeps everything else we know about each patient.

## Age groups

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 7.2** — Create `age_cat`: Under 18, 18-29, 30-39, 40-49, 50-59, 60-69, 70-79, 80+.
:::

```{r}
linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>%
  mutate(age_cat = case_when(
    age_years < 18 ~ "Under 18",
    age_years < 30 ~ "18-29",
    age_years < 40 ~ "30-39",
    age_years < 50 ~ "40-49",
    age_years < 60 ~ "50-59",
    age_years < 70 ~ "60-69",
    age_years < 80 ~ "70-79",
    age_years >= 80 ~ "80+"
  ))

linelist_clean %>% count(age_cat)
```

Because `case_when()` stops at the first TRUE line, `age_years < 30` only catches ages 18–29 (younger ages were already caught by the line above).

`count()` lists the groups in alphabetical order ("18-29" before "Under 18"). In Session 5 you will learn how to put them in a sensible order with factors.

::: callout-note
## 🔁 The base R way: `cut()`

Base R's `cut()` makes groups from numbers by giving the **break points**. `right = FALSE` means each group includes its lower limit (18 goes into "18-29"):

::: follow-along
**🔁 Follow along 7.3** — The same groups with `cut()`. Check with `table(useNA = "ifany")`.
:::

```{r}
cut(linelist_clean$age_years,
    breaks = c(0, 18, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, Inf),
    labels = c("Under 18", "18-29", "30-39", "40-49", "50-59", "60-69", "70-79", "80+"),
    right  = FALSE) %>%
  table(useNA = "ifany")
```

The same counts as `case_when()`, and already in the right order, because `cut()` returns a **factor** (Session 5). Forgetting `right = FALSE` is the classic mistake: then an 18-year-old lands in "Under 18".
:::

::: callout-warning
## Common mistakes

Ending with `TRUE ~ "80+"` (or `.default = "80+"`) puts every patient with a **missing** age into the 80+ group. Write the last condition out in full (`age_years >= 80 ~ "80+"`) so missing ages stay `NA`.
:::

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT 8 (4 min): outcome and age groups

In `measles_clean`:

a)  make `outcome` consistent with `str_to_title()`
b)  create `age_cat`: "Under 5", "5-9", "10-14", "15+"

✅ **Check:** `count(outcome)` shows only Died, Recovered, NA; `count(age_cat)` shows 4 groups plus NA (31)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution

```{r}
measles_clean <- measles_clean %>%
  mutate(
    outcome = str_to_title(outcome),
    age_cat = case_when(
      age_years < 5   ~ "Under 5",
      age_years < 10  ~ "5-9",
      age_years < 15  ~ "10-14",
      age_years >= 15 ~ "15+"
    )
  )

measles_clean %>% count(outcome)
measles_clean %>% count(age_cat)
```

"died" and "recovered" now match "Died" and "Recovered" (52 died, 1095 recovered, 68 missing). The 31 missing ages (the 27 "unknown" plus the four 999s) stay `NA` because the last condition is written out in full.
:::
:::

# Part 8: One pipeline and saving your work

Here is every step as **one** pipeline. This is the version to keep in a real project: one block that goes from raw data to clean data, so anyone can re-run it and get exactly the same result.

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 8.1** — One pipeline from `linelist_raw` to `linelist_clean`.

Pattern: `linelist_clean <- linelist_raw %>% clean_names() %>% rename(...) %>% mutate(...)`
:::

```{r}
linelist_clean <- linelist_raw %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  rename(
    date_of_infection = infection_date,
    onset_date        = date_onset,
    hospital_date     = hosp_date
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    # Types
    date_of_infection = as.Date(date_of_infection),
    onset_date        = as.Date(onset_date),
    hospital_date     = as.Date(hospital_date),
    date_of_outcome   = as.Date(date_of_outcome),
    age               = as.numeric(age),
    # Values
    age_years = if_else(age_unit == "months", age / 12, age),
    wt_kg     = if_else(wt_kg <= 0, NA, wt_kg),
    gender    = case_when(
      gender == "m" ~ "male",
      gender == "f" ~ "female"
    ),
    hospital_name = case_when(
      str_detect(hospital, "Central")           ~ "Central Hospital",
      str_detect(hospital, "Military|Mitylira") ~ "Military Hospital",
      str_detect(hospital, "Regional")          ~ "Regional Medical center",
      str_detect(hospital, "Mark")              ~ "St. Mark's Maternity Hospital",
      str_detect(hospital, "HMO")               ~ "HMO Health",
      str_detect(hospital, "Premier")           ~ "Premiere Health",
      .default = "Other/Unknown"
    ),
    # New variables
    bmi = round(wt_kg / (ht_cm / 100)^2, 1),
    bmi = if_else(bmi < 10 | bmi > 60, NA, bmi),
    age_cat = case_when(
      age_years < 18 ~ "Under 18",
      age_years < 30 ~ "18-29",
      age_years < 40 ~ "30-39",
      age_years < 50 ~ "40-49",
      age_years < 60 ~ "50-59",
      age_years < 70 ~ "60-69",
      age_years < 80 ~ "70-79",
      age_years >= 80 ~ "80+"
    )
  )

glimpse(linelist_clean)
```

Inside one `mutate()`, later lines can use columns made on earlier lines (`bmi` is created, then fixed).

## Save your work

`export()` is the opposite of `import()`. Save cleaned data to `processed_data/` — never over the raw file.

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 8.2** — Save `linelist_clean` as `processed_data/linelist_clean.rds`.

Pattern: `export(DATA, here("FOLDER", "FILE_NAME.rds"))`
:::

```{r}
export(linelist_clean, here("processed_data", "linelist_clean.rds"))
```

`.rds` is R's own file format. It keeps everything exactly as it is in R — dates stay dates and missing values stay `NA` — so it's the best choice for a file you will open in R again. (We compare `.rds` and `.csv` in Session 3.)

Session 3 starts from this file.

# Key points

-   The pipe `%>%` means "and then": `data %>% step_1() %>% step_2()` reads in order, left to right.
-   **Never edit the raw data file** — every fix happens in code, so anyone can re-run it.
-   `clean_names()` fixes every column name at once; `rename(new = old)` changes one.
-   `mutate()` creates or overwrites columns; `as.Date()` and `as.numeric()` fix types.
-   `if_else()` fixes values that meet one condition; `case_when()` handles many, checked in order. Use `NA` to blank out impossible values instead of deleting rows.
-   `str_detect()` and `str_to_title()` catch misspellings and inconsistent capitals; check every recode with `count(old, new)`.
-   Keep **one pipeline** from raw to clean data, and save the result with `export()` as `.rds` in `processed_data/`.

**Next: Session 3 — Missing Data, Joins, and Export.** We deal with rows that have no Case ID, duplicates, and missing values, join extra case information, and save the final datasets.
